      9. Integral limit theorems#

      We have already established the monotone convergence theorem, which allows the exchange of limits and integrals for non-decreasing sequences of non-negative functions: implies . In many applications, however, sequences of functions oscillate, take both positive and negative values, and lack any monotonicity. We wish to identify general conditions under which pointwise convergence almost everywhere guarantees convergence of integrals without requiring monotonicity.

      Pointwise convergence alone does not suffice. As we show in counterexamples, convergence of integrals may fail because ``mass escapes to infinity’’ or ``concentrates into a vanishing set’’. The Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem precludes this behavior by requiring the sequence to be bounded by a single integrable function, called a dominating profile.

      We will present two proofs: a simpler proof that relies on Fatou’s lemma for non-negative sequences without monotonicity assumptions, and a second approach that follows the philosophy described above, combining Egorov’s theorem on almost uniform convergence with the uniform integrability of the dominator to avoid ``concentration’’ and a standard tail estimate to avoid ``escape to infinity’’.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • State the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem and contrast its hypotheses with the monotone convergence theorem.

      • Construct sequences showing how limit-integral exchange fails when mass escapes to infinity or concentrates at a point, and analyze their minimal dominating profiles.

      • Formulate and apply Fatou’s lemma to sequences of non-negative measurable functions.

      • State and prove Egorov’s theorem using dyadic scales and explain why its finite-measure hypothesis is needed.

      • Prove dominated convergence using Fatou’s lemma, and alternatively using a finite-measure reduction, Egorov’s theorem, and uniform integrability.

      Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space, and pointwise equalities and inequalities are understood to hold -almost everywhere unless stated otherwise.

      These two examples isolate the two mechanisms that disrupt the convergence of integrals: mass spreading over sets of infinite measure (escape to infinity) and mass concentrating into sets of vanishing measure with unbounded amplitude (concentration). An integrable dominator prevents both behaviors simultaneously: by Markov’s inequality, has finite-measure superlevel sets (ruling out escape to infinity), and by Theorem 8, is uniformly integrable, meaning its integral on sets of small measure is uniformly small (ruling out concentration).

      9.2 A proof using Fatou’s lemma#

      The monotone convergence theorem requires the sequence to be non-decreasing. In practice, however, sequences of functions often oscillate and may fail to be monotone, or even fail to converge pointwise. Even when a pointwise limit does not exist, the limit inferior always exists in for every sequence of non-negative measurable functions. Fatou’s lemma provides a fundamental one-sided inequality relating the integral of the limit inferior to the limit inferior of the integrals, with no monotonicity assumptions.

      9.3 Dominated convergence via almost uniform convergence#

      In Proposition 2, the proof of dominated convergence for series rested on two observations:

      1. the sum outside a finite set is small because is a convergent tail;

      2. on the finite set , pointwise convergence is automatically uniform.

      On a general measure space , the first mechanism translates naturally: by Markov’s inequality, an integrable dominator is supported ``mostly’’ on a set of finite measure , with the tail integral arbitrarily small.

      However, the second mechanism encounters a major obstacle: on a general measure space, pointwise convergence almost everywhere does not imply uniform convergence, even when the ambient space has finite measure! To bridge this gap, we require a tool that extracts uniform convergence from pointwise convergence on finite-measure sets. This tool is Egorov’s theorem, which shows that pointwise convergence is ``almost uniform’’: it becomes uniform after removing an exceptional set of arbitrarily small measure.
